title: Proteomics and the Eye
abstract: In the post-genomic era, recent advances in protein chemistry, mass spectrometry, and bioinformatics are bringing a rapid and fundamental transformation to biological and medical research. In humans, ~20,000 protein-coding genes give rise to ~100,000 proteins and an estimated 1 million different protein modified forms [1]. The proteome, which consists of all proteins expressed in a cell, tissue, or organism, is the basic link between the genome and phenotypes of health and disease. Proteins function as enzymes, hormones, receptors, immune mediators, structure, transporters, and modulators of cell communication and signaling. The many forms of proteins arise from mutations, RNA editing, RNA splicing, and post-translational modification – the proteome has much greater complexity than the genome. A major goal of proteomics is to detect and measure the diversity of proteins, their isoforms, and the localization and interactions of proteins in order to discover biological mechanisms, biomarkers, drug targets, and pathways of disease. Proteomics is a vital step in the progress of science from genetics to proteomics and subsequently to translational research and clinical trials. Proteomics has come relatively late to the field of ophthalmology and vision science compared with areas such as cancer, cardiovascular, and neurology research. The eye is an emerging proteome that offers many new opportunities for discovery [2]. In this Focus issue, several groups of investigators present research and perspectives on proteomics and its applications to the understanding of eye disease. Primary open angle glaucoma is a leading cause of blindness and the subject of three papers in this issue. Sienkiewicz and colleagues used isobaric tags for relative and absolute quantitation (iTRAQ) to compare the proteome of the trabecular meshwork in eyes with and without glaucoma. Glycosylation, an important post-translational modification (PTM), was altered in the trabecular meshwork of subjects with glaucoma [3]. Bouhenni and Edward provide a useful overview of proteins found in anterior segment tissues that have been associated with different types of glaucoma [4]. For over a decade, Tezel has conducted proteomic investigations of glaucoma, with a focus on the posterior segment of the eye and glaucomatous neurodegeneration. She draws from her experiences to show the different approaches her group has taken to identify altered protein expression, PTMs, and protein interactions in experimental glaucoma [5]. Corneal dystrophies, which can lead to visual disability and blindness, must often be treated by penetrating keratoplasty. The corneal dystrophies that are associated with variants of transforming growth factor beta induced protein (TGFBIp) are not well understood. Poulsen and colleagues investigated differences in lattice corneal dystrophy type 1 caused by A546D substitution versus A546D/P551Q double substitution. The P551Q mutation had altered thermodynamic stability that accounted for the structural changes in TGFBIp [6]. Limbal stem cells are essential for regeneration of the cornea epithelium. Honore and Vorum review the limited work to date on stem cell markers and emphasize the need for proteomic approaches to understand limbal stem cell biology [7]. The tear film is a readily accessible fluid for biomarker analysis. Salvisberg and colleagues found a consistent association between elevated alpha-1 antichymotrypsin in tears and multiple sclerosis [8]. The human lens contains proteins that do not turn over during the lifespan. Truscott and Friedrich review the accumulation of PTMs and degradation of lens proteins with aging [9]. It is interesting to note that age-related changes in lens crystallins begin as early as the second decade of life. The vitreous may provide valuable clues to the pathogenesis of retinal diseases. In their Viewpoint, Mahajan and Skeie emphasize the potential that the vitreous proteome may have in the future for personalized therapeutics [10]. The systematic collection of eye tissues is fundamental for high quality scientific investigation. Skeie and associates describe a platform for the collection and storage of biological samples for proteomic studies [11]. O-GlcNAcylation, the addition of a single O-GlcNAc moiety to the hydroxyl and serine residues of proteins, was discovered in 1984 by Torres and Hart [12]. This basic and dynamic PTM is implicated in diabetic retinopathy. Hyperglycemia increases flux through the hexosamine biosynthetic pathway, which, in turn, upregulates O-GlcNAcylation. The number of tools to study O-GlyNAcylation is increasing and should facilitate our understanding of diabetic retinopathy [13]. Proteomic investigations of the eye show the great potential of proteomics in providing novel insights into the pathogenesis of specific eye diseases. In the recent literature, Feener and associates showed that the kallikrein kinin system plays a role in the increased vascular permeability that occurs in diabetic retinal edema [14]. Chaekady and colleagues used iTRAQ and LC-MS/MS to identify proteins that were increased and decreased in the corneal stroma in keratoconus [15]. Descriptive studies of the cornea [16], tear film [17], and ciliary body [18] have greatly increased the known proteome of the human eye. In order to facilitate further work on the proteome of the human eye, the Human Eye Proteome Project (HEPP) was founded in September 2012 as a component of the Biology/Disease-driven Human Proteome Project of the Human Proteome Organization [2]. The audacious goal of the HEPP is “to characterize the proteome of the human eye in health and disease in order to gain insight into the pathophysiology of eye diseases and to contribute to new preventive and therapeutic modalities for the prevention of visual disability and blindness” [2]. We hope that this collection of papers “Focus on Proteomics and the Eye” will help stimulate further exciting work in this rapidly expanding area of investigation.

title: Finding the culprit for the failure of the immune clock as time goes by
abstract: Over the last years, it became clear that circadian rhythms can have major influences on the immune system.1 Circadian rhythms refer to endogenous 24-h cycles that are driven by internal molecular clocks. The importance of this rhythmicity is highlighted by the estimation that at least 10–20% of all mammalian genes are controlled in a circadian manner.1 It is well known that leucocyte trafficking from the bone marrow to the circulation is controlled in a circadian manner, which is regulated by key clock genes like Bmal1 and Arntl.2,3 Disruption of this circadian rhythmicity increases the occurrence of disease-causing inflammation and aggravates various pathologies, both acute ones like bacterial infections and myocardial infarctions and chronic ones like atherosclerosis.1,4 A recent study by Blacher et al.5 in Nature Immunology highlighted the interesting notion that the circadian gene regulation is disrupted upon ageing. Ageing as well as the disruption of circadian rhythmicity are both associated with an increased incidence of various pathologies including cardiovascular diseases.6 One of the main underlying mechanisms for this increased age-related risk is a dysregulation of the immune function, resulting in increased inflammation.7 In their study, Blacher et al. isolated blood monocytes and bone marrow macrophages from young (2-month-old) and aged (20-month-old) mice every 4 h over a 24 h period to investigate the circadian rhythmicity in these cells. Consistent with previously published results,2 young Ly6Chigh monocytes showed a clear circadian trafficking from the bone marrow to the circulation. Interestingly, however, this circadian rhythm is lost upon ageing, as the amount of circulating cells in aged mice hardly changed during the day. Ageing also affected the functionality of the cells, as aged mice demonstrated a reduced survival upon exposure with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) compared with young mice. Even more interesting, LPS injection at ZT12 (lights off) in young mice resulted in an increased mortality compared with mice injected at ZT0 (lights on), a differential circadian-regulated effect that could not be observed in aged mice. In line with this, the phagocytosis of Escherichia coli particles by macrophages also showed a clear rhythmicity in cells from young mice, while this was not the case in cells from aged mice, again clearly demonstrating that the diurnal rhythmicity is lost with ageing. To further elucidate the underlying molecular basis by which this myeloid circadian rhythmicity is lost with ageing, they performed unbiased transcriptomics, again with 4 h intervals, comparing peritoneal macrophages from young and aged mice. Macrophages from young mice showed 680 genes that undergo rhythmic transcription, while aged macrophages only showed 53 rhythmic genes, clearly highlighting that circadian transcription is significantly disrupted in macrophages upon ageing. In line with the abrogated rhythmic phagocytosis upon ageing, it could be shown that phagocytosis-related genes (CLEAR network) are indeed strongly reduced in aged macrophages and they have lost their rhythmicity. Although core clock genes play a key role in regulating this rhythmicity, the expression of these genes was interestingly not altered upon ageing and can therefore not explain these observations. Other underlying mechanisms were therefore investigated. Although chromatin accessibility could not explain the loss of rhythmicity upon ageing, differential binding of transcription factors could be observed. To identify relevant transcription factors, three criteria were used: the differential chromatin access between young and aged macrophages, the differential binding to genes that show distinct oscillatory patterns upon ageing and the loss of rhythmic expression of the transcription factor upon ageing.5 Based on these three criteria, only one transcription factor could be identified, being Kruppel-like factor 4 (KLF4). Using an ex vivo approach, knockdown of KLF4 disrupted the bacterial phagocytosis and the diurnal rhythm of this phagocytic activity. Furthermore, using the UK BioBank, the authors observed that carriers of a KLF4 variant (rs2236599) have a striking increased risk of developing an E. coli infection and an enhanced infection-related mortality, while overall mortality is unchanged. In this specific biobank, age seems to play an important role as carriers of the KLF4 variant have a reduced age-associated risk for an E. coli infection. All in all, KLF4 seems to be a key regulating factor of the observed age-related circadian effects on macrophages. While this study elucidated the genetic regulatory pathways underlying the effect of ageing on circadian rhythmicity, additional mechanisms that result in a diminished KLF4 activity should be further explored in the future. Besides affecting macrophages, KLF4 can also influence non-immune processes, as it has also been identified as a key transcriptional regulator of mitochondrial homeostasis, including in the heart.8 Interestingly, mitochondrial function has also been described to be dysregulated upon ageing and this may accelerate the development of atherogenesis.9 Therefore, it would be interesting to investigate whether KLF4 is also a key regulator behind the age-related accelerated atherosclerosis and whether circadian effects may play a role in this. In line with this, loss of KLF4 or its family members (e.g. KLF2, KLF5, KLF15) in endothelial cells or smooth muscle cells results in vascular dysfunction and promotes atherosclerosis development.10 Since the exact effects of these KLFs on age-related circadian rhythms in vascular cells and vascular function remain elusive, these are interesting focus points for future research. Although Blacher et al. already initiated translation of their observations to humans in the setting of antimicrobial immunity, it would be highly interesting to further validate their findings using different cohorts of patients with various confounding factors including cardiac or vascular pathologies. This study also highlights the need to take into account the circadian rhythm in clinical studies that involve the isolation of cells such as peripheral blood mononuclear cells, as the time of day at which cells are collected may have an impact on the cells behaviour and thereby confound the outcome of the study. Similarly, therapies targeting macrophages and especially therapies that rely on phagocytosis by macrophages, should be performed in a timely fashion, keeping the circadian rhythm in mind to ensure optimal targeting. Taken together, the study by Blacher et al. provides crucial initial data showing an important interaction between ageing, circadian rhythmicity, and KLF4 in macrophages (Figure 1). This study opens the door to further investigate these interactions in other immune cells and in non-immune cells like the vascular cells. Future research should aim to elucidate potential targets that can be used to stimulate the circadian rhythmicity upon ageing, as this may contribute to an adequate immune response throughout the course of life. Ageing disrupts circadian gene regulation in a KLF4-dependent manner. Upon ageing the circadian rhythmicity of gene expression regulation is lost. This loss of circadian rhythmicity goes hand in hand with immune dysfunction and inadequate immune responses. Although more underlying mechanisms are likely and still need further exploration, KLF4 seems to be at least one of the key regulators. Figure has been created with BioRender.com. Biography: Dr Sandrine Lecour is a Full Professor at the University of Cape Town, Deputy Director of the Cape Heart Institute, University of Cape Town and leader of the Cardioprotection Group. Her research group focuses on the delineation of novel cardioprotective signalling pathways, including high density lipoproteins, sphingolipids, and melatonin. Over the past few years, part of her research has focused on the delineation of the Survivor Activating Factor Enhancement (SAFE) pathway, which is triggered by the immune system. She has published over 100 papers in peer-reviewed journals (H index = 45). She is on the Editorial Board of many peer-reviewed journals, including Journal of Molecular and Cellular in Cardiology and Basic Research in Cardiology. Prof Sandrine Lecour is a Fellow of the European Society of Cardiology and she has been a Committee Member of the European Society of Cardiology Working Group on Cellular Biology of the Heart (2011–21). She is currently the Treasurer at International Society for Heart Research, European section. As the co-founder and the President of the South African Society for Cardiovascular Research (SASCAR) (2009–16), she constantly strives to promote the research and training of students in the cardiovascular field in South Africa. Biography: Dr Emiel van der Vorst obtained his PhD in Cardiovascular Biology and Medicine from the Cardiovascular Research Institute Maastricht (CARIM), The Netherlands in 2015, by studying the effects of high-density lipoproteins on inflammation. For his postdoctoral period he investigated the role of chemokines and chemokine-receptors in atherosclerosis at the Institute for Cardiovascular Prevention (IPEK) in Munich, Germany, resulting in several high-impact publications. Since 2019, he is working as group leader at the Institute for Molecular Cardiovascular Research (IMCAR) in Aachen, Germany, as well as at CARIM and IPEK. Currently his research is focusing on elucidating various mechanisms by which the lipid metabolism interacts with the immune system in the context of cardiovascular disease, especially atherosclerosis. His work is funded by various prestigious (inter)national personal grants and he is member of the editorial boards of several cardiovascular focused journals. Furthermore, he is a nucleus member of the Scientists of Tomorrow from the European Society of Cardiology.

title: When spermatogenesis meets human aging and elevated body mass
abstract: Aging is a biological process that takes place naturally in all living organisms, and affects the physiology and functionality of almost all organ and tissue types, including the reproductive tracts. The ultimate impact of aging in reproduction differs in women and men: while women stop menstruation and ovulation at the age of around 50, men can maintain the ability to produce sperm for the vast majority of their lifetime. Diverse developmental trajectories of germline stem cells may lead to this difference in genders. Specifically, spermatogonial stem cells (SSCs) in the testis remain relatively constant all life, while germline stem cells analog SSCs in men unlikely exist in the adult ovary of women. Intriguingly, although many older men display declined fertility, certain individuals have relatively normal fertility status, as measured by sperm count. The factors responsible for such heterogeneity may be due to differences in individual genetic background, and diverse environmental exposures. Regardless, understanding how aging affects men’s fertility requires delineation of the detailed underlying molecular mechanisms as well as examination of the influence of potential associated factors such as lifestyle, which may provide new avenue to identify novel therapeutic targets or develop effective intervention options to improve the reproductive health of men. The integrity of testis physiology is critical for successful spermatogenesis, and germline cells are supported and guided by testicular somatic cells, including Sertoli cells (which nurture and support germ cells), Leydig cells (which produce testosterone), and the testicular peritubular cells (TPCs; which contribute to the basement membrane). Aging can lead to several physiological alternations in the testis, such as fibrosis, deposition of extracellular matrix, and increased basement membrane thickness [1]. Understanding the molecular mechanism underlying those changes is of great clinical and scientific significance. Leveraging the unique access to human testis samples through rapid autopsy, recent work took advantage of single cell transcriptomic profiling approach and examined changes in the key components in the human testis during human aging [2], revealing multiple altered pathways. These included elevated inflammation as a globally shared pattern among testicular somatic cells, dysregulated metabolic signaling in Sertoli cells, altered hedgehog signaling and testosterone production in Leydig cells, and improper cell growth in the TPCs. Moreover, while young fertile men share relatively consistent molecular signatures, different degrees of the molecular changes listed above are observed in older men, prompting further investigation into the consequences of those changes. How does this aging-related molecular dysregulation of testicular somatic cells impact spermatogenesis and fertility? The outcome seems to depend on the extent of the molecular disruption. Older men with relatively modest molecular alternations display complete spermatogenesis with normal fertility, while those with severe alternations exhibit spermatogenic defects. Human spermatogenesis starts with the differentiation of SSCs into differentiating spermatogonia, which enter into meiosis to give rise to spermatocytes, culminating in the formation of haploid gametes—sperm. Interestingly, based on histological examination and transcriptomic analysis, older men with spermatogenic defects typically have regressed germ cell differentiation but relatively intact SSCs, which display normal SSC transcriptomic signatures, indicating that SSCs are less responsive to changes caused by aging (Fig. 1). One possible interpretation is the “survivor bias,” i.e. SSC diminishment via apoptosis might be too swift so that only viable SSCs with “normal” transcriptomes can be captured. However, the SSCs in older men display high variations in colonizing efficiency when transplanted into the testes of immune-comprised mice, suggesting additional layers of aging-related regulation exist in these SSCs. For instance, older men may accumulate more genetic mutations in their SSCs, in which a small proportion can result in increased proliferation and the ability to outcompete their peers—a phenomenon termed spermatogonia selfish selection [3]. Another possible explanation is that SSCs in older men may experience changes in their epigenome (such as DNA methylation, histone modifications, and small RNA repertoire) in response to aging, which could also impact their function [6, 7]. It has been widely reported that epigenetic alternations take place in the gametes, which can be transmitted to the offspring and influence their health [8]. Here, it still remains elusive whether those epigenetic alternations take place prior to spermatogenesis—within the germline stem cells—or instead emerge during germ cell differentiation in the advanced germ cells. If these epigenetic changes indeed take place in SSCs, they may also impact SSC development and maintenance as spermatogenesis progresses. When one examines the genomics analyses alongside the morphological results, it becomes obvious that the testicular somatic cells display much more pronounced changes in transcription than the germ cells during human testis aging. Notably, Sertoli cell numbers declined significantly in older men, accompanied with diminished metabolic function. As another key testicular somatic cell type, Leydig cells display age-related dysregulation in testosterone production as well. Therefore, somewhat surprisingly, somatic cell aging appears to be the primary driver of testis aging that leads to abnormal fertility

title: Deciphering the Mechanisms Behind Cardiovascular Disease: Long Noncoding RNAs as Key Molecular Signaling Hubs and Biomarkers of Atherosclerosis
abstract: Despite decennia of intense and active research, the etiology of complex diseases, such as those of the cardiovascular system (CVD), still remains to be fully understood and elucidated. At a fundamental level, risk factors can be classified as modifiable or nonmodifiable, with modifiable lifestyle factors such as physical activity along with nutrition being pivotal to the healthy maintenance and aging of the cardiovascular compartment. Moreover, exercise and diet have been recognized as key modalities in the primordial, primary, and secondary prevention of CVD, and combined with pharmacotherapy, in the tertiary management, rehabilitation, and treatment strategies of these conditions. Similar to most biological processes, those of the cardiometabolic systems are maintained in a state of dynamic and finely regulated equilibrium. This universal principle, identified by Claude Bernard in the 19th century, enables stability and survival in a constantly changing environment. It ascertains the relative homeostasis of major physiological parameters, such as body temperature, heart rate, hemodynamic blood flow, oxygen saturation of blood and tissue, pH, glucose levels, and blood pressure.1 Underpinning these vital parameters lies composite and exquisitely regulated molecular mechanisms and integrative biochemical interactions, systematized to maintain cardiovascular homeostasis. Although a considerable degree of redundancy and shift in the balance from the equilibrium point can be tolerated, even necessary for our physiological adaptive ability and providing a window for plasticity, excessive perturbations in major homeostatic bounds can have negative consequences, giving rise to chronic vascular inflammation, cellular dysfunction, and atherosclerosis (AS). Aberrant vascular smooth muscle cell (VSMC) and endothelial cell (EC) function is a sine qua non for the development and progression of CVD, which is characterized by a lag time between onset and clinical manifestation. This temporal deterioration of functionality exemplifies the attempted autoregulation of events that occur when the equilibrium of the CVD is disturbed, implicating the “causality” principles of CVD risk factors and the role of epigenetics in the etiology of AS. This results in altered patterns of gene expression over the course of time, at both the cell and tissue specific level. These modifiable and dynamic changes in the transcriptome are not dependent on changes in coding DNA sequence itself but on the epigenome. These epigenetic changes are defined by a collection of chemical marks on DNA and histones that controls chromatin architecture and associated regulatory binding proteins. It is established during embryogenic development and modified throughout our lifespan by age and lifestyle. In addition, this fine-tuning molecular mechanism of transcription is further complimented by posttranscriptional control of gene expression, also defined as an epigenetic mechanism, and combined together play an important role in the (patho-) physiology of many disease states, including CVD. In this issue of the Journal of Cardiovascular Pharmacology, Xie et al eloquently identified the long noncoding RNA (lncRNA), LOXL1-AS1 as both a key molecular hub in the etiology of AS and a potential circulating diagnostic and/or prognostic biomarker. Technological advancements have enabled genomic and transcriptomic analysis with improved sensitivity and specificity. It has been elucidated that ncRNAs constitute approximately 98% of the transcriptome. Major strides in this new field in genomics have led to the identification and classification of different types of ncRNAs and quantification of their expression in different tissues and disease states. Deciphering the permutations and combinations of ncRNA expression profiles, along with advices in functional genomics, such as CRISPR (clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats) and Cas9 (CRISPR-associated protein-9) recombinant technology, with bioinformatic data analysis, has identifying ncRNA as key regulators of gene expression, fine-tuning biological processes, and homeostasis.2–4 In addition, growing evidence indicates that ncRNAs interact and coregulate each other. microRNAs (miRNAs) are evolutionarily conserved across species, emphasizing their many important functions. These diverse biological processes include cell cycle progression, proliferation, apoptosis, immunity, metabolism, and development. They are characterized as single-stranded ncRNAs of 17–27 nucleotides in length, fine-tuning gene expression by posttranscriptional silencing of specific target RNAs. Their effector function is elicited by a number of defined mechanisms. They may repress translation by mRNA targeting through their 5′ seed region (6–8 nucleotides). This in itself is not sufficient complementary nucleotide pairing to induce target mRNA cleavage but may interfere with the ribosome translational machinery. High compliment pairing between miRNAs and 3′ miRNA response elements located in the 3′UTR of target RNAs mediates RNA interference pathways through cleavage in the RNA-induced silencing complex. This combinatorial regulatory property of miRNA allows a single miRNA to have hundreds of different mRNA targets and a single gene transcript to be regulated by multiple miRNAs.5 lncRNAs are a class of RNA transcripts, more than 200 nucleotides in length, that lack any predicted coding sequence or ability. Nearly 60,000 human lncRNAs have been annotated to date and seem to exhibit strong tissue specificity, both in expression and functionality. Functional in vitro and model organism studies of the ever growing (l)ncRNA repertoire have demonstrated that they are involved in many biological pathways and (patho-)physiological processes at the epigenetic and transcriptional level. Therefore, defining the function of human lncRNAs will provide important insights into physiology and disease biology. lncRNAs act as molecular scaffolds for proteins interacting with transcription factors (TFs) or chromatin-modifying complexes to modulate gene transcription.3 In addition, lncRNAs may also act as competing endogenous RNAs (ceRNAs) whereby miRNAs and lncRNAs regulate each other through their biding sites.6 Interactions of miRNAs and lncRNAs have been reported to trigger degradation of the targeted lncRNAs and also to sequester miRNA, thus playing an important role in target gene expression. These interactions form complex, integrated and coregulatory networks, involving lncRNAs, miRNAs, small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs), and PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs) to regulate gene expression. Xie et al present their findings and discuss the newly identified positive feedback loop between the lncRNA LOXL1-AS1, the miRNA miR515-5p, and the TF signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (STAT3). This work is timely in that, in contrast to our expanding knowledge regarding the function of lncRNAs, the molecular intricacies regarding their mechanisms of action are largely unknown. Although protein-coding genes are largely conserved in mammals, the overwhelming majority of human lncRNAs is nonconserved and believed to be lineage specific. Although the low conservation of genomic sequences often suggests a limited or lack of function, emerging evidence supports that some nonconserved human lncRNAs clearly have functionality. The fact that some lncRNAs display structural but not sequence conservation emphasizes our lack of understanding of the mode of lncRNA conservation, making it challenging to elucidate lncRNA functionality and “modus operandi” in vivo. lncRNA LOXL1 antisense RNA 1 (lncRNA LOXL1-AS1) was first identified in the pathogenesis of the pseudoexfoliation (PEX) syndrome.7 Subsequently, it has been found to be an oncogenic lncRNA in many cancers, correlated with tumor size, distant metastasis, histological grade, and survival time. It regulates diverse cell functions, such as proliferation, cell cycle, migration, and invasion. Loss-of-function studies in osteosarcoma cell lines demonstrated knockdown of LOXL1-AS1 dramatically inhibited osteosarcoma cell proliferation, migration, and invasion through suppressing the PI3K-AKT signaling pathway.8 Mechanistically, LOXL1-AS1 acts through crosstalk and coregulation of various miRNAs and their associated signaling pathways. Xie et al found elevated levels of LOXL1-AS1 in the plasma of AS patients, highlighting its potential use as a CVD biomarker. Interestingly, in the context of CVD, LOXL1-AS1 expression has previously been demonstrated to be increased in response to both oxidative stress and cyclic mechanical stress in various human cell lines.9 Using in vitro techniques, Xie et al have identified LOXL1-AS1 as a functional lncRNA in both human VSMCs and ECs. Downregulation of LOXL1-AS1 was shown to inhibit proliferation and migration. This knockdown also promoted apoptosis in VSMCs and human umbilical vein ECs (HUVECs). Upregulation of LOXL1-AS1 was found to be through STAT3, a TF that mediates cellular responses to a variety of cytokines and growth factors. Both receptor and nonreceptor tyrosine kinases activate STAT3 by phosphorylation and dimerization. This is mediated through phosphorylation of JAK2, an intracellular nonreceptor tyrosine kinase. Dimerized STAT3 translocates to the nucleus, where it activates a variety of genes associated with cell growth, survival, and motility. Furthermore, LOXL1-AS1 was found to positively regulate STAT3 expression and was mainly distributed in the cytoplasm of VSMCs and HUVECs. This led Xie et al to hypothesize that LOXL1-AS1 regulates STAT3 expression through sponging miRNA, acting as a ceRNA. Through bioinformatic target prediction and molecular approaches, miR515-5p was identified and validated to bind with LOXL1-AS1 and STAT3 in VSMCs and HUVECs. In addition, LOXL1-AS1 could upregulate STAT3 expression by sequestering miR515-5p. A synopsis of the studies highlights are illustrated in Figure 1.FIGURE 1.: Diagram outlining the involvement of the lncRNA LOX1-AS1 in the etiology of AC. Increased expression levels of lncRNA LOX1-AS1 as a result of extrinsic risk factors, sequesters the miRNA miR515-5q by acting as a ceRNA. This results in a positive feedback loop, which facilitates EC and VSMC proliferation and migration, both hallmarks of AC (illustrated by R.P.M). JAK, Janus tyrosine kinase; NF-kB, nuclear factor kappa-light-chain-enhancer of activated B cells; P, Phosphorylated; RISC, RNA-induced silencing complex; SRC, Src kinase family, non-receptor tyrosine kinases.This study highlights the potential role of ncRNAs as circulating functional biomarkers of CVD and maybe used to refine CVD diagnosis, treatment, and management strategies. Importantly, as key molecular hubs in CVD, developing novel therapeutics targeting ncRNA's involvement in AS has the potential to change the treatment landscape, facilitating more effective and targeted solutions. Although challenging to develop, they potentially will have applications for a wide range of diseases that are not effectively addressed with existing therapeutics.10

title: Cancer and epigenetics – basic research and clinical implications: Joint Meeting of the Fourteenth International Symposium of the Hiroshima Cancer Seminar and the Eighth Meeting of the Tottori Bioscience Promotion Foundation, October 2004
abstract: The Joint Meeting of the Fourteenth International Symposium of the Hiroshima Cancer Seminar (HCS) and the Eighth Meeting of the Tottori Bioscience Promotion (TBP) Foundation was held on 30–31 October 2004 at the International Conference Center, Hiroshima. The symposium consisted of 12 special lectures and 34 free paper presentations for poster session; approximately 250 people were present and actively discussed topics relating to cancer and epigenetics, from basic research to clinical implication. Prior to this symposium, an Open Lecture to the public by HCS was held on 30 October. Kazunori Kodama (Radiation Effects Research Foundation, Hiroshima) spoke about cancer prevention to more than 120 people. To begin the meeting, Eiichi Tahara (Radiation Effects Research Foundation, Hiroshima), Chairman of the HCS Foundation, gave an opening address. Tahara introduced a brief background and the purpose of this series of symposia. Since the establishment of the HCS Foundation in 1992, annual international symposia are organized to create an opportunity for basic scientists and clinical researchers to exchange ideas for cancer research, cancer prevention and cancer therapy. This year, the organizing committee planned to explore the important issue of ‘Cancer and Epigenetics’. The epigenetic mechanism is deeply involved in the pathogenesis of human cancers. CpG island methylator phenotypes (CIMP) might be one of the major pathways responsible for the development of gastrointestinal cancer. Because inactivation of various suppressor genes by promoter methylation or chromatin modification commonly occurs in human cancers, these may provide potential targets for therapeutic intervention. The participants profit by exchanging and learning ideas from informative presentations and discussions, and also contribute to future development in cancer treatment and prevention. Jean-Pierre Issa (University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, USA) delivered a lecture, entitled ‘Bedside epigenetics’, and described the impact of epigenetic process in tumorigenesis and cancer management. Epigenetic changes in cancer consist of primary DNA methylation changes, as well as histone code changes related to DNA methylation or abnormalities in specific histone modifying enzymes. The field is rapidly moving towards clinical applications in patients with cancer, including risk assessment, early detection, prognostication and therapeutic targeting. In colorectal cancer, methylation in normal appearing mucosa appears to increase with age and to be particularly pronounced in patients with advanced preneoplastic and neoplastic lesions. Measurement of methylation in normal appearing mucosa could therefore predict the risk of cancer development, as will be argued for the MGMT gene. In multiple tumor types, a high degree of CIMP appears to be associated with a poor prognosis following standard management. In colorectal cancer, the presence of CIMP in patients who present with stage IV disease is associated with a short survival following 5-fluorouracil based therapy. Drugs that inhibit DNA methylation (5-azacytidine and 5-aza-2’-deoxycytidine, or DAC) are now used in clinical trials for various malignancies. Data suggest that, in myeloid malignancies, the efficacy of DAC is greater at low doses that favor hypomethylation over cytotoxicity, and that responses require the induction of in-vivo hypomethylation. Overall, it seems clear that epigenetic processes will have a significant and varied impact on the management of neoplasia in humans. Mitsuo Oshimura (Tottori University, Yonago) described the epigenetic regulation in imprinted domains in cancer. Genomic imprinting, the phenomenon whereby mono-allelic expression of certain genes occurs depending on their parental origin, plays an important role in mammalian development, growth and cell differentiation. Disturbance of normal imprinting is frequently associated with various types of cancer. LIT1 is an imprinting control center at human chromosome 11p15.5. Several lines of evidence suggested that LIT1 transcript regulates chromatin modifications, resulting in alteration of gene expression in the domain in some, but not all cancer cells. The human paternally expressed gene 3 (PEG3) on chromosome 19q13.4 is one of the candidate tumor suppressor genes for glioma. It has been identified that three expressed sequence tags (EST), H80201, H78825 and AW197312, exhibit paternal allele-specific expression, using human monochromosomal hybrids containing a paternal or maternal origin of PEG3 locus. The EST H80201 was expressed only from the paternal allele in normal lymphoblasts by using a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP). Monoallelic expression of EST H80201 was also detected in non-tumor adult brain tissues of gliomas. These EST were located directly adjacent to PEG3 in a head-to-head orientation. This new transcript, imprinted transcript 1, is located upstream but oriented opposite to PEG3 (ITUP1). Bisulfite sequencing and reverse transcription (RT)-PCR indicated that hypermethylation of the promoter correlated with the absence of these transcripts. ITUP1 and PEG3 may be coordinately regulated, and down-regulation of both genes could be important in the development of glioma. Hidenobu Soejima (Saga University, Saga) presented on the epigenetic regulation of LIT1 imprinting domain and its implication in human diseases. To clarify the chromatin-based imprinting mechanism, the histone modification status at a differentially CpG methylated region of LIT1 (DMR-LIT1) was investigated. Mice harboring targeted deletion of DMR-LIT1 on the paternally inherited chromosome and microcell hybrids harboring targeted deletion of human DMR-LIT1 resulted in the de-repression of imprinted genes including KIP2, indicating that DMR-LIT1 is an imprinting control region for the domain. This region is demethylated in half Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome (BWS) patients and in several tumors. Chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) assays revealed that in both species, DMR-LIT1 with the CpG-methylated, maternally derived inactive allele showed histone H3 Lys9 (H3K9) methylation, whereas the CpG unmethylated, paternally active allele was acetylated on histone H3/H4 and methylated on H3 Lys4 (H3K4). In the BWS patients with DMR-LIT1 imprinting defect, H3K9 methylation disappeared completely. Furthermore, in esophageal cancer cell lines, expression of imprinted KIP2 gene was statistically correlated with loss of CpG methylation at DMR-LIT1, not with KIP2 promoter methylation itself. Loss of CpG methylation at DMR-LIT1 was also associated with loss of H3K9 methylation. These findings suggest that the histone modification at DMR-LIT1 plays an important role in imprinting control within the imprinting domain, and that loss of histone H3K9 methylation together with CpG demethylation on the maternal allele might lead to the BWS phenotype and might be involved in esophageal cancer. Satoshi Fujii (Hiroshima Red-Cross Hospital, Hiroshima) described the role of histone modification in the imprinted tumor suppressor gene. ARHI is a maternally imprinted tumor suppressor gene whose expression from the paternal allele is markedly down-regulated in breast cancer in addition to loss of heterozygosity. Consistent with imprinting, all three CpG islands of ARHI gene were partially methylated in normal human breast epithelial cells. Reactivation of ARHI expression in breast cancer cell lines by CpG demethylating agents and/or histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors was related to the methylation status of the CpG islands in the ARHI promoter, especially CpG island II. ChIP assays revealed that treatment with a CpG demethylating agent and/or HDAC inhibitor could increase ARHI expression in breast cancer cells, with a corresponding increase in histone H3K9/18 acetylation and decrease H3K9 methylation. The similar experiments were performed in mouse A9 hybrid cell lines containing only a single maternal (A9–1M) or paternal (A9–1P) allele of human chromosome 1. The histone H3K9/18 acetylation level at ARHI was much higher in A9–1P cells than in A9–1M cells. By contrast, A9–1M cells had much higher H3K9 methylation levels at ARHI than did A9–1P cells. Only treatment with a combination of HDAC inhibitor and a demethylating agent reactivated the imprinted allele. These data suggest that parental allele-specific DNA methylation, histone H3 acetylation and H3K9 methylation are key regulatory mechanisms in ARHI imprinting. Yutaka Kondo (University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center, USA) gave a talk on the role of histone modifications in tumor suppressor genes in cancers. The status of histone modification at silenced tumor suppressor gene loci was examined in colorectal cancers. DNA methylation and histone modifications (H3K4 undermethylation, H3K9 underacetylation and H3K9 hypermethylation) were closely correlated at silenced loci in colorectal cancers. Treating cells with inhibitors of HDAC and inhibitors of DNA methylation resulted in large effects on the histone code associated with reactivation of gene expression, suggesting that the sequence of loss of histone acetylation followed by gain of histone methylation on H3K9 is needed for silencing. Next, to evaluate the global distribution of target genes silenced by H3K9 methylation in cancer, a human CpG island microarray was probed with DNA obtained by ChIP using anti H3K9 methylated antibody or anti H3K9 acetylated antibody. Eleven genes, one EST, two unknown fragments and 13 repetitive sequences were identified as targets of H3K9 modification. In addition, a strong correlation was found between the ratio of K9 methylation/acetylation and DNA methylation in those clones. To examine the mechanisms of aberrant histone methylation and which histone methyltransferases may be involved, RNAi-based inhibition of histone methyltransferase, SUV39H1, G9a and EZH2 expression was studied. The preliminary data show that treatment of cancer cells with RNAi to SUV39H1, G9a and EZH2 potentiates gene reactivation, markedly inhibits cell growth and causes profound morphological changes in cancer cells. Mitsuyoshi Nakao (Kumamoto University, Kumamoto) described the role of methylated DNA-binding proteins in transcription and genomic stability. DNA methylation contributes to genome regulation including control of gene expression and chromatin structure. Genome stability is also linked to this epigenetic modification. In the nucleus, the methylated DNA is recognized by methylated DNA-binding domain (MBD) proteins. There are at least five mammalian MBD proteins: MeCP2, MBD1, MBD2, and MBD3 for transcriptional repression, and MBD4 (also known as MED1) for mismatch repair as a thymine glycosylase. Among them, MBD1 acts as a transcriptional regulator through the cooperation of MBD, cysteine-rich CXXC domains, and a C-terminal transcriptional repression domain (TRD). The MBD of MBD1 recruits histone methyltransferase Suv39h1, HDAC1/HDAC2 and HP1 that can bind methyl H3K9. MBD1-containing chromatin-associated factor 1 (MCAF1), also known as the human homolog of murine ATFa-associated modulator (AM), interacts with TRD of MBD1. It is particularly noted that MCAF1/AM converts dimethyl to trimethyl H3K9 by histone methyltransferase SETDB1/ESET. These data indicate that MBD1 may tether Suv39h1-HP1 and SETDB1-MCAF1 complexes to methylated DNA regions, suggesting the presence of pathways from DNA methylation to histone methylation for epigenetic regulation. Furthermore, MBD1 is involved in genome integrity by cooperating with methyl-purine DNA glycosylase, one of the key molecules in the base excision repair. Issay Kitabayashi (National Cancer Center Research Institute, Tokyo) reported the function and regulation of the AML1 transcription factor complex. Specific chromosome translocations are frequently found in human leukemia and often result in the expression of fusion gene products. The genes encoding the AML1/CBF transcription factor complex are the most frequent targets of these translocations. The AML1 complex contains histone acetyltransferases such as p300 and MOZ, promyelocytic leukemia (PML), a corepressor mSIN3A and a protein kinase (AML1K). MOZ and p300/CBP stimulates AML1-dependent transcription. In contrast, a leukemia-associated fusion MOZ-CBP inhibited AML1-mediated transcription and inhibits differentiation of M1 myeloid cells. A specific isoform of PML (PML I) was able to recruit AML1 and coactivator p300 in PML nuclear bodies and enhance the AML1-mediated transcription in the presence of p300. Overexpression of PML I stimulated myeloid cells to differentiate into neutrophils. These results suggest that PML I could act as a mediator for AML1 and its coactivator p300/CBP to assemble into functional complexes, and consequently, activate AML1-dependent transcription and myeloid cell differentiation. AML1K mediated phosphorylation of AML1, p300 and MOZ. AML1K stimulated HAT activity of p300 and transcription activation by GAL4-p300. AML1K strengthened interaction between AML1 and MOZ. The genes encoding AML1 and some of the AML1-interacting proteins are the targets of leukemia-associated chromosome translocations, suggesting that common pathways may be shared by distinct myeloid malignancies and underscores the importance of this complex in hematopoiesis and leukemogenesis. Toshikazu Ushijima (National Cancer Center Research Institute, Tokyo) focused on genome-wide screening techniques for differences in DNA methylation between two genomes. His group previously developed methylation-sensitive-representational difference analysis (MS-RDA). The advantage of MS-RDA is that it focuses on unmethylated and CpG-rich regions of the genome, and thus differential methylation of unique CpG islands can be intensively screened, avoiding interference by repetitive sequences. In an analysis of human stomach cancer, they identified silencing of nine genes, Lysyl oxidase (LOX), H-ras like suppressor (HRASLS), bA305P22.2.3, Filamin-c (FLNc/g-filamin/ABPL), HAND1, a homolog of RIKEN2210016F16, FLJ32130, Peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor g angiopoietin-related (PGAR/HFARP/ANGPTL4/ARP4) and Thrombomodulin (TM), as a result of methylation of 5′-CpG islands. Among the nine genes, growth-suppressive activities had been reported for LOX and HRASLS in ras-transformed fibroblasts and for TM in melanoma cells. Tumor-suppressive activities of LOX and HRASLS were examined in gastric cancers by introducing their cDNA into gastric cancer cell lines. Introduction of LOX successfully suppressed cellular growth, colony formation in soft agar, and tumor growth in nude mice, while that of HRASLS did not. These results indicate that LOX is a novel tumor-suppressor gene in human gastric cancers. The power of methylation-based genome-wide screening was impressive. Victor V. Lobanenkov (National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, USA) presented epigenetic regulation of human genome universally involving CTCT/BORIS-binding regions. Many human pathologies including cancer and imprinting disorders may involve common types of epigenetic deregulations non-randomly distributed throughout genomes. It is hypothesized that an ‘epigenetic havoc’ often observed in such pathologies, including LOI in tumors that exhibit regional genome-wide demethylation with a narrower site-specific hypermethylation, might be associated with a common particular malfunction of the DNA-targeting mechanisms necessary for the proper localization and functional reading of epigenetic marks. Such targeting should involve sequence-specific DNA-binding factors, but their identity remained elusive until CTCF-binding regions have emerged as the most likely places of epigenetic modifications in mammals. The duplicated ‘multivalent’ 11 Zn-finger DNA-binding domains (11ZF-DBD), which comprise one-third of the total length in the two paralogous nuclear factors of similar size, CTCF and BORIS, appear to conduct the DNA-targeting part in the molecular orchestra of normal and aberrant epigenetic marking in mammals. Unlike normal somatic cells with CTCF, the vast majority of cancer cells are found to abnormally coexpress CTCF and BORIS together. Several studies of the IGF2/H19 LOI, caused by altering normally mono-allelic CTCF-binding in tumors by aberrant bi-allelic hypo- or hyper-methylation of at least one of several CTCF-sites in the H19 ICR, suggested that CTCF and its targets are taking the central stage in human cancer (epi)genetics. An ongoing mapping of the 11ZF-DBD-binding sites with gel-shifts and verifying each novel site for methylation-sensitive CTCF versus BORIS binding in vivo, strongly supports an idea that misdirected epigenetic regulation in already developed tumors is mediated through a misuse of varying sequences recognized by the 11ZF-DBD. Hidetoshi Tahara (Hiroshima University, Hiroshima) gave a talk on genetic and epigenetic regulation of cell cycle genes in human aging. Cellular senescence causes cells to arrest proliferation, essentially irreversibly, by induction of cyclin dependent kinase inhibitors such as p16INK4a and p21waf1. title: Highlighted Research Articles
abstract: Xu, Deng, Liu, Zhuo, Zhu, Chang, Liu, Fu, Li, Liu, and colleagues launched a multicenter, prospective, single-arm, phase II clinical trial and included 34 patients with PD-L1+, persistent, recurrent or metastatic cervical cancer to receive first-line de-escalated platinum-based chemotherapy plus anlotinib and penpulimab, followed by maintenance therapy solely with anlotinib and penpulimab. They reached an objective response rate of 93.8%. Multiomic analysis demonstrated that heightened chemotaxis and proliferative activity of tumor-infiltrating T cells and activated germinal center B cells informed optimal treatment response. Higher TLS-to–tumor area ratio was correlated with improved survival. These findings lay the foundation for the feasibility of first-line de-escalated chemotherapy plus immune-targeted therapies for the clinical management of patients with metastatic, persistent, or recurrent cervical cancer.See article, p. 439.An understanding of tumor cell dynamics can inform prognosis and treatment decisions but remains limited in lung adenocarcinoma in never smokers (NS-LUAD). Using RNA sequencing from 684 NS-LUAD tumors with independent validation, Zhao and colleagues identified three robust molecular subtypes with distinct cellular programs, genomic features, and survival outcomes. These subtypes differed in proliferation, differentiation, and tumor cell states and composition, resulting in marked prognostic differences, even among stage I tumors. A 60-gene signature recapitulates the classification and predicts survival even within subgroups based on tumor stage or established genomic features, highlighting its potential clinical utility in early-stage NS-LUAD.See article, p. 460.Patients with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) develop acquired cystic kidney disease (ACKD) and renal tumors, yet the causal biology is unclear. To investigate this, Takahashi, Tanaka, and colleagues performed integrated spatial immunogenomic analysis of 268 specimens, revealing that ESRD-associated tumors are molecularly distinct from sporadic renal cell carcinoma. ACKD exhibited an inflammatory microenvironment, and renal cysts developed from proximal tubular cells that survived inflammation and expanded clonally, while microenvironmental signals drove paracrine MET activation to support tumorigenesis. These data define pathogenic circuits in ESRD and suggest preventative strategies.See article, p. 478.Huang, Hagihara, and colleagues profiled 1,582 intestinal metaplasias (IM) across six countries with varying gastric cancer incidence, identifying recurrent driver mutations, IM-specific mutational signatures, and Helicobacter pylori variants associated with regional gastric cancer risk. Matched blood analyses demonstrated that clonal hematopoiesis (CH), associated with age and smoking, was independently associated with progression to dysplasia and gastric cancer. CH carriers showed greater abundance of oral bacteria within IM regions, suggesting disruptions in host mucosal immunity. These findings pave the way for molecularly stratifying patients with IM by their future gastric cancer risk and point to potential targeted prevention strategies for IM.See article, p. 497.Loss of the tumor suppressor PTEN is a frequent driver of aggressive, treatment-resistant cancers, yet targeted therapies remain elusive. Tang, Zhou, and colleagues identified a novel mechanism by which PTEN loss induces aberrant phosphorylation of PI3Kβ at tyrosine 962. This event triggered the formation of an oncogenic EPHA2–SRC–PI3Kβ signaling complex. Targeting this phosphorylation, either genetically or with dasatinib, suppressed tumor growth in PTEN-deficient models. These findings position phospho-PI3Kβ Y962 as a druggable vulnerability and predictive biomarker, offering a strong rationale for new therapeutic strategies and biomarker-guided repurposing of dasatinib in PTEN-null solid tumors.See article, p. 521.Wang and colleagues show that the developmental timing of oncogenic mutations fundamentally shapes leukemia biology. Using genome engineering, the authors introduced the leukemia-driving fusion, NUP98::NSD1, into human blood stem cells from fetal, postnatal, pediatric, or adult stages. Fetal-derived stem cells transformed readily into aggressive leukemia, whereas later-stage cells became increasingly resistant. Single-cell analyses revealed that fetal-origin leukemia stem cells were more quiescent, metabolically distinct, and associated with poor patient outcomes. Importantly, these cells exhibited specific vulnerabilities that could be therapeutically targeted. This study establishes ontogeny as a key determinant of leukemic potential and provides a framework for developmental stage-informed precision therapy.See article, p. 541.Cellular senescence is a damage-induced program with contrasting tumor-suppressing and -promoting functions, the determinants of which are not fully understood. Zhou and colleagues found that senescence arises not only within tumor cells, but also in stromal populations in mouse and human prostate cancers. p21 marked senescent stromal cells with an inflammatory senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) that promoted myeloid-mediated immune suppression and drove prostate tumorigenesis. Removal of stromal p21+ cells blocked tumor progression and activated T-cell immunity, potentiating anti–PD-1 immunotherapy in prostate cancer. These findings pave a path to target detrimental senescent cells in cancer to improve therapy outcomes.See article, p. 571.An important question in cancer pathogenesis is whether a genetic mutation is required for disease initiation, disease maintenance, or both. Here, Köhnke, Karigane, and colleagues examined this question in human acute myeloid leukemia (AML), where DNMT3A R882 missense mutations often arise early. They developed CRISPR-based methods to prospectively correct DNMT3A R882 mutations directly in primary patient cells. Using this approach, they find that DNMT3A R882 mutations were necessary for AML initiation and increased leukemia stem cell frequencies but were largely dispensable for maintenance. These findings disentangle initiation and maintenance roles of DNMT3A R882 mutations and showcase prospective functional cancer genetics in primary human cells.See article, p. 592.

title: What’s New in Musculoskeletal Basic Science
abstract: Musculoskeletal basic science provides a foundation for clinical knowledge while fostering innovation in the management of orthopaedic conditions. In the past year, several outstanding articles have been published that advance our understanding of neural system function and its crosstalk with immunity in tissue healing and regulation of bone homeostasis, revealing new roles of mechanotransduction in bone and critically assessing vitamin D supplementation in schoolchildren (6 to 13 years of age). Novel research was generated on maintaining muscle strength and function, establishing the role of synovium in chronic inflammatory joint pathology, and the effects of aging on the musculoskeletal system. These publications provide new insight into the physiologic and pathologic processes underlying orthopaedic conditions and critically assess routine clinical practices with high-level evidence. All 20 musculoskeletal science articles chosen for this review were published in extremely prestigious, high-impact-factor journals. Somatic and Autonomic Innervation Physical activity requires precisely coordinated participation of the somatic nervous system controlling skeletal muscles and the autonomic nervous system enabling synchronous responses from the inner organs. Although somatic and autonomic innervations have separate anatomic representations, the nature of their coordinated interactions remains elusive. Zhang et al.1 discovered that spinal-projecting neurons in the rostral ventromedial medulla (rVMM) simultaneously coregulate both somatic motor and autonomic sympathetic activity in different bodily functional states. Using adeno-associated virus (AAV) retrograde tracing and optogenetic mapping, spinal-projecting neurons located in the gigantocellular reticular nucleus alpha (GiA) and ventral part (GiV) of the rVMM exhibited axon collaterals connecting the motor and sympathetic spinal neurons. These spinal-projecting neurons exhibited excitatory or inhibitory regulation of skeletal muscle tone concurrently with sympathetic tone (blood pressure, heart rate). Active states such as exercise exhibited spinal-projecting neuron excitation causing high motor and sympathetic tones, whereas quiescent states such as sleep showed spinal-projecting neuron inhibition yielding skeletal muscle atonia and sympathetic hypoactivity. This study considerably advances our knowledge on neuronal circuitry governing coordinated motor and sympathetic responses during different functional states. Neuroimmune Modulation of Tissue Healing Nociceptive sensory neurons are important immunoregulators exerting protective or damaging effects via neurogenic inflammation. The neuroimmune interactions during tissue healing following an injury are poorly understood. Lu et al.2 demonstrated that ablation of the Nav1.8 voltage-gated sodium channels in nociceptive neurons in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) impaired healing of full-thickness skin wounds and regeneration of volumetric muscle loss. Transgenic Nav1.8cre/Rosa26DTA mice lacking Nav1.8 exhibit impaired sensory axon ingrowth into granulation tissue, which coincides with local downregulation of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP). CGRP released by the Nav1.8+ neurons enables skin and muscle healing by interacting with CD11b+ myeloid cells via receptor activity-modifying protein 1 (RAMP1). CGRP upregulates thrombospondin-1 (TSP-1) in neutrophils and monocytes/macrophages to inhibit their recruitment and enhance efferocytosis and M2 polarization. Mice with diabetic neuropathy (Leprdb/db), similar to Nav1.8-deficient mice, exhibit reduced CGRP expression in sensory neurons and impaired tissue-healing, which can be mitigated with exogenous local CGRP delivery. The study demonstrated that tissue-healing involves complex CGRP-mediated neuroimmune interactions and suggested potential new treatment options. Regulation of Bone Homeostasis A demand for high calcium levels in breast milk during lactation causes abrupt bone loss. In mechanistic studies, Babey et al.3 identified cellular communication network factor 3 (CCN3) as a potent osteoanabolic hormone released in the early postpartum period throughout lactation. CCN3 is secreted from the kisspeptin-positive neurons of the arcuate nucleus (ARCKISS1+) in the brain. Parabiosis of female wild-type mice and female mice overexpressing CCN3 (Esr1Nkx2-1-cre) revealed the same high bone mass. Further, human stem cells exposed to CCN3 showed enhanced osteogenic differentiation and matrix mineralization, regardless of cell donor age and sex. Systemic CCN3 delivery augmented the bone phenotype in ovariectomized mice and reversed the skeletal sequelae of a chronic high-fat diet known to compromise ARCKISS1+ neurons. Finally, localized CCN3 delivery enhanced femoral osteotomy healing in aged female and male mice. Knocking down Ccn3 in the arcuate nucleus leads to excessive bone loss during lactation, further compounded by a low-calcium diet. The study identified maternal CCN3 as a potent brain-derived, osteoprotective hormone released during lactation and delineated its osteoanabolic properties. Osteoclastogenesis controls bone turnover, although several pathways regulating the process remain unclear. Colocalization of osteoclast precursors with eosinophils in bone marrow suggests their interaction. Andreev et al.4 discovered that eosinophils regulate osteoclast activity in both normal and pathologic bone conditions. Eosinophil-deficient ΔdblGATA knockout mice exhibit a marked reduction in bone mass due to increased osteoclastogenesis. Conversely, eosinophilia in transgenic interleukin (IL)-5 mice strongly inhibits osteoclast differentiation and activity by altering their transcriptional profile. Eosinophil peroxidase (EPX) was identified as a regulator of osteoclast formation and function by downregulating mitochondrial reactive oxygen species (ROS) and mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPKs) in osteoclast precursors. EPX treatment ameliorated bone loss induced by inflammatory arthritis and estrogen deprivation. In humans, the number and the activity of eosinophils highly correlated with bone mass in healthy participants and patients with rheumatoid arthritis. This study revealed a novel function of eosinophils to regulate bone homeostasis and underscored the role of innate immunity in the process. Mechanotransduction in Development, Health, and Disease Postnatally, mechanical signals dynamically regulate skeletal homeostasis and its adaptive changes; however, the role of mechanical cues in embryonic skeletal development is largely unknown. Collins et al.5 established the essential role of Hippo signaling and its downstream transcription factors YAP (Yes-associated protein) and TAZ (transcriptional coactivator with PDZ-binding motif) in fetal murine osteoblasts and their coordinated interactions with endothelial cells during embryonic endochondral ossification to form bone. In transgenic mice, selective YAP/TAZ deletion in osteogenic osterix (Osx)-expressing cells causes loss in mechanoresponsivness due to alteration of gene expression required for cell cytoskeleton rearrangement to sense mechanical stimuli. YAP/TAZ spatially couple Osx+ osteoblast precursors with endothelial cells of sprouting vessels to initiate cartilage hypertrophy and remodeling at the endochondral ossification centers, thereby mechanoregulating bone formation in murine developing limbs. Single-cell transcriptomics revealed a specific population of vessel-associated osteoblast precursors, and YAP/TAZ deletion in these cells downregulated C-X-C motif chemokine 12, which mediates vascular morphogenesis. Ex vivo bioreactor-based mechanical stimulation of explanted embryonic (E15.5) mouse hindlimbs increased mineralization, and YAP/TAZ deletion abrogated load-induced osteogenesis at the ossification sites. The study reveals a key role of YAP/TAZ in mechanosignaling during embryonic bone development, with potential implications for skeletal pathologies associated with fetal akinesia or hypokinesia and uterine crowding. Daylight is the primary entrainer of circadian rhythms, pacing and resetting the neuronal signals in the brain. Food intake, ambient temperature, and stress can uncouple circadian rhythms at autonomous tissue and organ levels. In a murine mechanistic study, Dudek et al.6 demonstrated that cyclic mechanical loading and resultant tissue osmolarity changes can reset the circadian rhythm phase and amplitude in femoral head articular cartilage and intervertebral disc devoid of innervation and vascularity. Using treadmill exercise in PER2::Luc reporter mice, they established that hyperosmolarity alone can effectively shift and reset the internal clock in young and aging skeletal phenotypes by modulating the expression of specific circadian rhythm genes. Transcriptomic and biochemical analyses revealed the PLD2-mTORC2-AKT-GSK3β molecular pathway as a convergent mechanism mediating both the loading-induced and hyperosmolarity-induced clock entrainments. These results demonstrate a key role of cartilage mechanoresponsiveness in synchronizing skeletal circadian rhythms and suggest cartilage osmolar intervention options. Altered mechanoresponsiveness was implicated in bone fragility in type-2 diabetes mellitus due to detrimental effects of a high-glucose and high-fat diet on osteocytes. Shao et al.7 demonstrated that unilateral in vivo tibial cyclic loading (1,200 cycles per day for 2 weeks) fails to improve bone mass, microarchitecture, and strength in genetically spontaneous (KK-Ay) and high-fat-diet combined with streptozotocin (HFD/STZ)-induced mice with type-2 diabetes mellitus. The lack of bone mechanoresponsiveness was directly associated with attenuated Ca2+ oscillatory dynamics in osteocytes mediated by a reduced expression of the SERCA2 pump. This process involves peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor α (PPARα), leading to fewer and weaker Ca2+ spikes with prolonged Ca2+ uptake in osteocytes with the type-2 diabetes mellitus phenotype. The loading-dependent Ca2+ oscillations cause immediate actin network contractions, thereby modulating osteocyte secretory activities (RANKL, OPG, SOST). Conversely, treatment with istaroxime, a SERCA2 agonist, improves bone mechanoresponsiveness by rescuing osteocyte Ca2+ dynamics in both type-2 diabetes mellitus models. Similarly, conditional osteocyte-specific SERCA2 overexpression (SERCA2flox/flox; DMP1-Cre) mitigated the type-2 diabetes mellitus-related suppression of bone mechanoresponsiveness. The study provided a mechanistic insight into compromised bone mechanoresponsiveness in type-2 diabetes mellitus and identified osteocyte Ca2+ signatures as druggable targets. Bone and Its Blood Supply Transcortical vessels connect the endosteum with periosteum to permit molecule and cell trafficking between the inner medullary and external bone compartments across the osteocyte-populated cortex. Liao et al.8 revealed a unique role of osteocytes, which, via rich direct dendritic connections with transcortical vessels, transfer mitochondria to the endothelial cells to protect them from oxidative stress, and promote their proliferation and migration, thereby enhancing transcortical vessel formation. The ablation of osteocytes in transgenic (Dmp1Cre-DTAki/wt) mice exhibits substantial reduction in transcortical vessel density and connectivity, resulting from significant downexpression of angiogenic genes (Vegfc, Slit3, Notch3, Notch4). The osteocyte-endothelium transfer of Dendra2-labeled mitochondria was visualized in vitro and in vivo and was required for transcortical vessel formation and functionality. The metabolic effects of the endothelial mitochondria uptake involved induction of D-sphingosine catalyzed by sphingosine kinase 1 (SPHK1). In vivo delivery of osteocyte-derived mitochondria or D-sphingosine (2 mg/kg for 7 days) enhanced intact femoral bone mass, density, and microarchitecture, and augmented diaphyseal defect healing in mice. These findings identify a unique mitochondria transfer regulating transcortical vessel formation and homeostasis. The pathways orchestrating synchronous new vessel formation and osteogenic stem cell recruitment and migration during bone-healing lack thorough understanding. In a dynamic imaging study, Bixel et al.9 employed intravital multiphoton microscopy to longitudinally surveil vascularization in murine calvarial defect healing and determined that initial microvessel (CD31+ Emcn+) formation did not spatially or temporally associate with osteoprogenitors (Osx+ Runx2+) emerging from the periosteum. Second-harmonic generation imaging permitted simultaneous visualization of angiogenesis and osteogenesis in double-transgenic Flk1-GFP and SP7-mCherry reporter mice. The early-formed vessels did not connect with the adjacent uninjured vessels, but rather with the outer periosteal and meningeal vasculature, and the blood flow velocities were highly variable and independent of the vessel diameter. Compared with femoral fracture-healing, the uncoupling of angiogenesis from osteogenesis was unique to calvarial healing. In contrast to femoral fracture-healing, the angiogenesis-related and hypoxia-related genes (Hif1a, Vegfa, Angpt2) were only slightly expressed in calvarial healing, and surprisingly, although they profoundly altered vascular ingrowth, endothelial Notch and vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) signaling did affect calvarial healing. The study represented a pioneering effort in sequential intravital imaging of the entire process of calvarial bone repair at a multiscale level and delineated highly dynamic relationships between angiogenesis and osteogenesis. Vitamin D Supplementation in Schoolchildren Vitamin D is a hormone promoting bone mineralization, specifically in the growing skeleton. Severe and prolonged vitamin D deficiency causes rickets and requires vitamin D therapy; however, routine vitamin D supplementation in children lacks evidence. Recently, 2 sister subtrials were reported, both nested within 2 separate main Phase-3 randomized clinical trials (RCTs). In the subtrial by Ganmaa et al.10 involving a secondary analysis of the outcomes of an RCT conducted in Mongolia, 8,851 schoolchildren (6 to 13 years of age) were randomized to receive weekly oral 14,000-IU vitamin D3 (4,418 schoolchildren) or placebo (4,433 schoolchildren) for 3 years and fracture incidence was assessed. At baseline, 31.9% of the schoolchildren were vitamin D-deficient ( 50 nmol/L). At the trial end point, schoolchildren in the vitamin D group had normalized vitamin D levels (mean, 72.1 nmol/L), whereas, in the placebo group, vitamin D status remained insufficient (26.1 nmol/L); nevertheless, fracture incidence was similar in the vitamin D group (6.4%) compared with the placebo group (6.1%). Alterations in blood parathyroid hormone (PTH), alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and minerals were noted only in vitamin D-deficient children. The subtrial by Middelkoop et al.11 was nested within the ViDiKids trial and assessed the effect of weekly oral 10,000-IU vitamin D3 compared with placebo for 3 years on bone mineral content (BMC) and serum calcium, vitamin D3, and PTH levels, bone remodeling markers (ALP, C-terminal telopeptide of type I collagen [CTX], procollagen type I N-propeptide [P1NP]), and fracture incidence in 450 Black African schoolchildren (6 to 11 years of age) from South Africa. At baseline, 5.8% of participating schoolchildren were vitamin D-insufficient (<50 nmol/L), and, at the trial end point, serum vitamin D3 was higher in the vitamin D group compared with the placebo group (mean difference, 39.9 nmol/L), whereas serum PTH was lower (mean difference, 0.55 pmol/L). There were no differences in BMC by dual x-ray absorptiometry (DXA) (whole body less the head; lumbar spine), serum calcium, or bone turnover markers. Fracture incidence was very low in both groups (0.93% compared with 1.32%). The null findings of these subtrials indicate that vitamin D supplementation alone does not reduce fractures or improve BMC or serum remodeling markers in schoolchildren despite vitamin D deficiency or insufficiency.
